extracted.intended_audience: journalism students and newspaper reporters (local/feature reporters)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and exemplars for writing various newspaper items (municipal finance, market reports, short human-interest pieces, and longer narrative/feature stories) as found in a newspaper/textbook section titled 'Types of News Writing.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Business / municipal bond reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Report sale details (amount, purchaser, premium, effective interest rate), list bidders and comparative bids, break down the issue by loan purpose/maturities/percentages, and interpret market significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include precise figures and percentages (e.g., '$1,000,000', premium of $5,670, interest rate 4.30%), show the bid prices (100.567, 100.44, etc.), itemize the composition of the issue with maturities and rates (municipal building loan, 20 years, 4 per cent, $200,000; etc.), and add expert or bureau commentary to place the sale in market context ('The rate at which these bonds were sold shows that the state of the money market is not as far from normal...'). Mention tax status and investor implications (tax exempt, exemption extending to federal income tax) and name local representatives/agents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Financial reporting on corporate dividends
rubrics_metrics.description: State declared dividends and compare them to historical norms and capital/earnings figures; explain causes of changes and operational impacts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide the declared rate (semi-annual dividend of 1 per cent), contrast with usual/dividend history (usual 4 per cent; since 1910 paid 7 per cent yearly), quantify the monetary effect (reduced amount $2,400,000), situate within company structure (which lines are operated, who owns stock), and explain reasons given by directors (e.g., 'chiefly to a large decrease in traffic and a material reduction in the revenues of the lines west of Pittsburgh'). Note regulatory rate decisions affecting business (interstate commerce commission freight decisions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Market/pricing reports (produce, meat, fish, dairy, poultry)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide precise, itemized price listings with units and origin notes; mention seasonality, supply sources, wholesale vs. retail differences, and trends vs. prior periods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List items with current prices and units (e.g., 'peaches ... by the dozen, good peaches 10 to 25 cents'; 'green corn 20 to 25 cents a dozen ears'; 'sirloin steak 33 to 38 cents retail'), indicate origins/shippers (Georgia, New Jersey, Connecticut, California), explain freight/packing costs and their effect on local prices, distinguish wholesale and retail behavior, and include stock/inventory figures when available (cold storage packages/cases). Give consumer guidance (insist on sweetness and flavor; avoid half-rotten fruit) and explain market mechanics (big crop but not low retail prices due to retailer margins).

rubrics_metrics.name: Local-news brief / municipal reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Convey succinct local developments (leases, building plans, company organization) with specific names, locations and intended uses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State concrete facts: site frontages, floors/purposes (first floor office, reading-room, public dining-room; eleventh story sample-rooms), construction details (fireproof, concrete floors, tile/marble in public rooms), materials and stylistic notes (limestone and brick in French Renaissance), and name principals and corporate officers (Commonwealth Associates, Inc.; George U. Crocker, president). Such specifics give authority and color to municipal notices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short human-interest / anecdotal reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Use vivid scene-setting, direct dialogue, strong leads, and character detail to tell a compact, engaging anecdote.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open with an immediate scene or action ('When a clerk at the desk ... picked up the desk telephone ... he caught the words of the operator'), include quoted speech that reveals character and voice (dialect or colloquial lines are acceptable to convey personality), describe physical actions and reactions (pounding the desk, elevator door flying open), and close with a punch or small resolution. Keep the narrative tight and rely on sensory/detail to engage readers (hotel clerk episode, subway guard routine, mirage at Far Rockaway, sailor mistakenly taken to prison).

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative/feature storytelling (longer colorful pieces)
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct longer, dramatized features that blend historical background, chronology, character sketches, and episodic scenes to build a story with suspense and color.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use an evocative lead and scene-setting (dawn, muffled hawseholes, specific place names), supply historical context and time shifts (220-year hiatus, 1684 Good Faith), combine documentary touches (ship's bell inscription, shipping registers, lawyers' names) with present-day action (sponge diver finds coins, forms expedition), name participants (Harvard/Yale alumni, owners) and organizational details (Southern Research Company), and build a plot arc (expedition assembling, rival plot). Employ descriptive language and narrative pacing to sustain reader interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of local specificity and sourcing
rubrics_metrics.description: Anchor stories with concrete local detail, named sources, firm names and places to lend credibility and relevance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include street names, firm names and representatives (e.g., 'Codman & Street, Easton Building', 'N. W. Harris & Co', 'Percy O. Dorr'), market sources (Boston News Bureau), and quantitative records. Attribution and named local sources help explain significance and provide verifiability.
